name: H-Store
tagline: Brown/MIT/CMU/Yale main-memory, partitioned OLTP research system that became VoltDB.
description: H-Store was an experimental distributed main-memory OLTP database built by Brown, MIT, Carnegie Mellon and Yale, following Stonebraker et al.'s 2007 argument that classic disk-based architectures waste most of their time on buffering, latching, locking and logging. Data is split into partitions, each owned by a single-threaded execution engine that runs pre-declared stored procedures serially, so single-partition transactions need no locks; durability comes from replication plus command logging. Later research added anti-caching to disk, automatic partitioning design and transaction prediction. A Java front end drives a C++ execution engine. The ideas were commercialised as VoltDB (now Volt Active Data); the H-Store code is archived.
statusNote: Research prototype (2007–2016); repository archived. Commercialised as VoltDB, now Volt Active Data.
developer: Brown University, MIT, Carnegie Mellon University, Yale University

scale.notes: Shared-nothing partitions across a cluster; data must fit in aggregate memory unless anti-caching is enabled.

strengths: Lock-free serial execution per partition for single-partition transactions
Command logging plus replication instead of heavyweight ARIES logging
Anti-caching research for data larger than memory
Widely cited codebase with benchmarks (TPC-C, SEATS, AuctionMark)
weaknesses: Archived research code with no support
Requires all transactions as pre-declared stored procedures
